title: Visualizing Icechunk stores
text:
Open a store in xarray
import icechunk, xarray as xr

url = "https://data.source.coop/ocean-icechunks/hycom/hycom-gofs-3pt1-reanalysis"
repo = icechunk.Repository.open(icechunk.http_storage(url))

# The data live in HYCOM's bucket, outside the store: allow reads from there.
auth = {p: icechunk.credentials.HttpAccess for p in repo.config.virtual_chunk_containers}
repo = repo.reopen(authorize_virtual_chunk_access=auth)

ds = xr.open_zarr(repo.readonly_session(tag="v1").store, consolidated=False, chunks=None)

From the snow crab notebook in chapter 1, which ran end to end on 2026-11-13. Opening the 306 TB store takes about a second, because only metadata is read.

title: Visualizing Icechunk stores
text:
Then it is just xarray

Bottom temperature in the Bering Sea, 15 July 2010, from the HYCOM store. The black line is 2 °C; the magenta box is the snow crab grounds.

title: Visualizing Icechunk stores
text:
Icechunk is built on Zarr

Zarr is an open format for chunked arrays in object storage. Each chunk is fetched on its own, with a simple web request
Icechunk stores Zarr arrays, and adds versions and commits on top
So any Zarr reader with Icechunk support can open these stores, in any language, straight from the bucket. No server in between




Where
Libraries




Python
icechunk + zarr + xarray, as in this tutorial


JavaScript (browsers)
zarrita + icechunk-js

section: gridlook: a store on a globe
text:
gridlook: a store on a globe
gridlook is a WebGL viewer for Earth system model output, built on zarrita and icechunk-js. Give it a store’s URL, and it draws the data on a globe in your browser, with nothing to install.
Open the ocean acidification indicators in gridlook →

Axes but no data? The browser also needs CORS on the source host. NCEI and the NDVI bucket send it; HYCOM’s bucket on AWS does not.


The OA indicators store is virtual: metadata from Source Cooperative, data from NCEI. Use the Depth slider to move through its 14 levels. The HYCOM viewer shows axes but no data in an ordinary browser for this reason.

title: Auditing your files
section: A virtual store is only as consistent as its files
text:
A virtual store is only as consistent as its files
Nothing is rewritten, so the files’ layout is the store’s layout.

A virtual store copies no data. So it can fix metadata, but it cannot fix how the bytes are laid out: the grid, the chunks, the compression. An audit tells you, before you build, whether the files will make a good store, a slow one, or several stores.

title: Auditing your files
text:
Consistent grids

Same dimensions, shape and coordinate values in every file, apart from the time dimension you join along
Files on different grids cannot share one array. They become separate groups, or separate stores


CoastWatch Ocean Heat Content: three regions on three different lat/lon grids, so three separate stores.

title: Auditing your files
text:
Consistent chunking

A chunk is the smallest piece a reader can fetch. Virtual stores keep the provider’s chunks exactly
Every file needs the same chunk shape for a variable
Unchunked arrays mean every read pulls the whole array


NOAA NDVI: NDVI is chunked 1 × 1200 × 2400, but QA in the same file is unchunked, so any read of QA pulls all 3600 × 7200 values.

title: Auditing your files
text:
Consistent encoding

Same dtype, compression, fill value and file format in every file
NetCDF-3 and NetCDF-4/HDF5 need different parsers, and cannot be mixed in one array
Check the file’s own header. Catalogs and servers get this wrong


PacIOOS: the servers implied HDF5, but the files were NetCDF-3. About 3,200 “replacement” files were compressed HDF5 under the same names.

title: Auditing your files
text:
Built to be appended

New files arrive the same way: same naming, same folder pattern, same grid
Each file’s length along time is a whole number of chunks. If not, an append can put data in the wrong place without any error
One time step per file works, but the time coordinate needs explicit chunking or the store opens slowly


CEFI daily files: 365 or 366 days each, chunked 100 days. In a test with that layout, appending put 430 of 730 values in the wrong place, with no error.

title: Auditing your files
text:
Bugs in the data

Missing time steps. Is it a real gap, or the product’s normal cadence?
Duplicated or out-of-order time steps
Empty, truncated or unreadable files
Coordinates that are all zero or all NaN


HYCOM GOFS 3.1: a few analyses are missing from the archive, so the snow crab notebook takes the nearest time that exists.

title: Auditing your files
text:
Missing or wrong metadata
This is the one thing a virtual store can fix, without touching the data.

Missing units, standard_name, long_name, or a vertical positive
Attributes that cannot be saved as JSON, such as a NaN fill value on a coordinate
No version recorded anywhere in the files


Fix it in the store, write down every change, and make the result follow CF conventions.

title: Auditing your files
text:
Look for yourself
import h5py, s3fs

fs = s3fs.S3FileSystem(anon=True)
url = sorted(fs.ls("noaa-cdr-ndvi-pds/data/2000"))[0]   # one day's file
with fs.open(url) as f, h5py.File(f) as h:
    for name, v in h.items():
        print(name, v.dtype, v.shape, "chunks:", v.chunks, v.compression)
...
NDVI int16 (1, 3600, 7200) chunks: (1, 1200, 2400) gzip
TIMEOFDAY int16 (1, 3600, 7200) chunks: (1, 1200, 2400) gzip
QA int16 (1, 3600, 7200) chunks: None None

Run on the first NDVI file on 2026-11-13. This reads only the header, a few kilobytes. Do this on files from the start, the middle and the end of the archive, and on both sides of any change in instrument, version or format.

title: Auditing your files
section: Let the agent write the audit report
text:
Let the agent write the audit report
First, tell it how to find the files. It cannot guess:

Where they are: a bucket and prefix, a THREDDS catalog, an API
How to get in: public, or which credentials
What to include: products, variables, years

Then ask:

“Audit the NOAA CDR NDVI files in s3://noaa-cdr-ndvi-pds/data/ (public, us-east-1, one NetCDF per day) for a virtual Icechunk store. Check grids, chunking, encoding, whether they can be appended, missing days and metadata. Read headers only. Write the findings to audit/report.md. No build code.”


The virtual-icechunk skill’s research-and-plan step does this audit. For a big archive, or files on a provider’s own server, the archive-to-cloud skill’s source audit scans everything resumably and reports what nobody asked about.

title: Working with an agent
section: From writing the code to directing the work
text:
From writing the code to directing the work


My own rough estimate, not a measurement. Without an agent, 80% of my time went to writing and debugging code. With one, I write almost none. Half my time is defining the task and the approach; the rest is directing and refining the work, and reviewing the code and text that come back.

title: Working with an agent
section: An agent is not a chatbot
text:
An agent is not a chatbot

It reads your files, runs commands and writes code in the folder you start it from
It asks before it does anything risky. Read the request before you say yes
It works in your name, with your subscription and your GitHub login


Treat it like a fast, well-read collaborator who is new to your project. Give it clear tasks, and check its work.


Set up in the JupyterHub Skills pages: “Start your coding agent” installs Claude Code, Codex or Antigravity and the ocean-icechunks skills.

title: Working with an agent
section: One task, one session, one handoff
text:
One task, one session, one handoff





%%{init: {"flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "padding": 14}, "themeVariables": {"fontSize": "20px", "fontFamily": "Inter, sans-serif"}}}%%
flowchart LR
  A["Pick a task"] --> B["Plan first"] --> C["Build small"]
  C -- "done?" --> E["Write a<br/>handoff note"] --> F["/clear"] --> A







The biggest mistake is treating the agent like a chat: tangents and one endless conversation. Every session gets one task with a boundary.

title: Working with an agent
text:
A task has a boundary







A task
Not a task




“Check whether these HYCOM files allow byte-range reads”
“Help me with Icechunk”


“Write a plan for a virtual store of the NDVI files”
“Let’s work on the data”


“Make the smoke-test notebook read real values”
“Make everything better”


“Explain why this store shows axes but no data”
“Tell me about Zarr”

title: Working with an agent
text:
Plan first, build small

Ask for a plan before any code. Claude Code has a plan mode (Shift+Tab) that stops it from changing files while it plans
Read the plan. That is where your science knowledge matters most
Build one small piece at a time: one notebook, a few files, one check. Small pieces are easy to review, and cheap to redo

title: Working with an agent
text:
Close the loop
When a task is done, or you are switching tasks, or the session is getting long:

“I am about to clear. Write what we did and what’s next to notes/handoff.md.”
Type /clear
Start the next task with “Read notes/handoff.md and continue.”


Long conversations cost you three ways: they use up your subscription faster, the agent loses focus, and a crash loses everything since the last note.

title: Working with an agent
text:
What a skill is

A folder of instructions (SKILL.md plus reference files) that teaches the agent how to do one kind of job
The agent reads every installed skill’s one-paragraph description at the start of a session
When your request matches, it loads the skill and follows it


You do not call a skill. Describe the task in plain language, and the agent picks the skill. To ask for one directly, type /virtual-icechunk (in Codex, $virtual-icechunk).

title: Working with an agent
text:
ocean-icechunks-skills







Skill
Use it to




virtual-icechunk
Research, build, validate, document and audit virtual Icechunk stores of NetCDF/HDF5 files


archive-to-cloud
Copy a provider’s files, unchanged, to object storage first, when they are not somewhere a store can reference



Both were written from lessons learned on real ocean-data builds, and they work with Claude Code, Codex, Copilot and Antigravity.
Install them: Start your coding agent → Add the ocean-icechunks skills
github.com/ocean-icechunks/ocean-icechunks-skills

title: Working with an agent
section: The skill builds in a set order
text:
The skill builds in a set order





%%{init: {"flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "padding": 14}, "themeVariables": {"fontSize": "20px", "fontFamily": "Inter, sans-serif"}}}%%
flowchart LR
  A["1 · Research<br/>and plan"] --> B["2 · Smoke-test<br/>notebook"] --> C["3 · Production<br/>build"] --> D["4 · README and<br/>loading example"]







It stops for your review between steps. Expect questions and a plan before any build code
The smoke test writes to a local store and must read real data back
Credentials never go in a notebook, and tests never touch a production store

title: Working with an agent
text:
Prompts that work
I want a virtual Icechunk store for the NOAA CDR NDVI files in
s3://noaa-cdr-ndvi-pds. Research the files and write a plan before any code.

Does this THREDDS server expose the real NetCDF files, or only OPeNDAP?

Write a smoke-test notebook that builds a small store from three of these
files and reads real data back.

The smoke test passed. Turn it into a production build script.

Write the README and a loading example for this store.

Why is this store so slow to open?

title: Working with an agent
text:
You are still the scientist

Check the numbers. Do the values, units and dates make sense for this dataset?
Ask why. “Why did you drop that variable?” “What did you assume about the time axis?”
Stop it when it goes in circles. A build that keeps failing gets more expensive, not more likely to work

title: Working with an agent
text:
Report a lesson back
A skill only knows what someone has written into it. When a build teaches you something:

Ask: “What did this build teach that the virtual-icechunk skill should know?”
Write it down in your project’s notes, with the evidence
Open an Update skill issue

title: Working with an agent
text:
Try it
In a terminal on the hub:
mkdir -p ~/ndvi-store && cd ~/ndvi-store
claude          # or codex, or agy
Then ask: “Research the NOAA CDR NDVI files for January 2000 in s3://noaa-cdr-ndvi-pds and write a plan for a virtual Icechunk store. No code yet.”

Read the plan together. Does it find the files are NetCDF4/HDF5? That the files are one day each? Does it notice the QA variable is unchunked? Chapter 4 covers what an audit should find.

title: The scratch bucket
text: The hub comes with an S3 scratch bucket. It is a good place to write a test Icechunk store to cloud storage, rather than to your home directory. You do not need to set up any credentials, because the hub already has them.

title: The scratch bucket
text:
Your folder
The hub sets an environment variable, SCRATCH_BUCKET, that points to a folder named after your GitHub username:
import os
scratch = os.environ["SCRATCH_BUCKET"]
scratch    # 's3://<scratch-bucket>/<your-github-username>'

title: The scratch bucket
text:
Write, list, read and delete
import s3fs

fs = s3fs.S3FileSystem()             # uses the hub's credentials

fs.pipe(f"{scratch}/hello.txt", b"hello")   # write a small file
fs.ls(scratch)                              # list your folder
fs.cat(f"{scratch}/hello.txt")              # read it back
fs.rm(f"{scratch}/hello.txt")               # delete it
To upload a local file or folder, use fs.put("local.nc", f"{scratch}/local.nc"). For a folder, add recursive=True. fs.ls raises an error on an empty folder, so write something first.

title: The scratch bucket
section: An Icechunk store in the scratch bucket
text:
An Icechunk store in the scratch bucket
You can write an Icechunk store here almost as easily as to a local folder. Only the storage setup changes:
import boto3
import icechunk

bucket, prefix = scratch.removeprefix("s3://").split("/", 1)
creds = boto3.Session().get_credentials().get_frozen_credentials()   # the hub's credentials

storage = icechunk.s3_storage(
    bucket=bucket,
    prefix=f"{prefix}/my-store",
    region="us-west-2",
    access_key_id=creds.access_key,
    secret_access_key=creds.secret_key,
    session_token=creds.token,
)






Note



Why not from_env=True? On this hub, Icechunk does not pick up the hub’s credentials by itself, and you get AccessDenied (tested 2026-11-13 with icechunk 2.3.1). Passing them from boto3 works. They expire after about an hour, so rerun the cell if a long session starts failing.


Chapter 5, Building a store, covers the rest. Or ask your agent: “write the smoke-test store to my scratch bucket instead of a local folder.”
Adapted from NMFS HackDays 2025: Using the S3 Scratch Bucket.

title: Start your coding agent
text:
In this hackathon you hand most of the work to a coding agent running in a hub terminal. Bring your own subscription. Any one of these works:
You install the agent once. It goes in ~/.local/bin, inside your home directory, so it is still there the next time your server starts. Your sign-in is saved there too.

title: Start your coding agent
text:
1 · Install and sign in
Open a terminal (File → New → Terminal). Then follow the steps for your agent.

Claude CodeCodexAntigravity


Install:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Start it:
cd ~
claude
The first start asks you to pick a theme and a sign-in method. Choose Claude account with subscription. It prints a link: open it in your browser, sign in, and paste the code it gives you back into the terminal.


Install it into your home directory. Without --prefix, it is installed somewhere that is wiped when your server restarts.
npm install -g --prefix ~/.local @openai/codex
Sign in. The hub has no browser of its own, so use the device-code flow:
codex login --device-auth
Open the link it prints, sign in with your ChatGPT account, and enter the code. Then start it:
cd ~
codex


Install:
curl -fsSL https://antigravity.google/cli/install.sh | bash
Start it:
cd ~
agy
On the first start, sign in with the Google account that has your Antigravity access. It prints a link: open it, sign in, approve, and paste the code back into the terminal.



When you see the agent’s prompt, type /exit to leave. You only needed it installed and signed in.






“Command not found”?



Open a new terminal, so it picks up ~/.local/bin. If that does not help, run export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" and try again.

title: Start your coding agent
text:
2 · Add the ocean-icechunks skills
The ocean-icechunks-skills teach your agent how to build, check and document virtual Icechunk stores. This installs them for all three agents at once:
git clone https://github.com/ocean-icechunks/ocean-icechunks-skills ~/ocean-icechunks-skills

for dir in ~/.claude/skills ~/.agents/skills ~/.gemini/config/skills; do
  mkdir -p "$dir"
  for skill in virtual-icechunk archive-to-cloud; do
    ln -sfn ~/ocean-icechunks-skills/skills/$skill "$dir/$skill"
  done
done
To update them later, run git -C ~/ocean-icechunks-skills pull.

title: Start your coding agent
text:
3 · Start it where you work
An agent works in the folder you start it from. So always cd into your project first:
cd ~/my-project
claude        # or codex, or agy
The first time you start it in a new folder, it asks whether you trust the folder. Say yes for your own project folders.
Check that the skills loaded. Type /skills (in Claude Code or Codex) or / (in Antigravity) and look for virtual-icechunk. Or just ask: “What skills do you have for Icechunk?”
Chapter 2, Working with an agent, covers how to get good work out of it.

title: Log in to the JupyterHub
text: Everything in this tutorial runs on a JupyterHub in the cloud. You do not need to install anything on your own computer.

title: Log in to the JupyterHub
text:
Start a server

Go to https://workshop.nmfs-openscapes.2i2c.cloud/.
Log in. Your username is your email address. The password is the one the organizers give you at the start of the hackathon; everyone uses the same one. Do not post it anywhere public, including GitHub.
Image: keep the default, a geospatial image with Python and R.
Size: pick the smallest machine. That is plenty for everything here. Larger machines cost more, so choose one only if you run out of memory.

Click Start. It can take a few minutes to start.

When it is ready you land in JupyterLab, on the Launcher. Next: Find your way around JupyterLab.

title: Log in to the JupyterHub
text:
Your files

/home/jovyan is your home directory. Everyone’s home is called /home/jovyan (that is the Jupyter default), but yours is private, and it persists between sessions.
shared/ is read-only, with files the organizers have put there for you.
shared-public/ is read-write and visible to everyone. Make a team folder there. Agree with your team who edits what, because anyone can change anything in it.

title: Log in to the JupyterHub
text:
Stop your server
When you are done for the day, stop your server. It shuts down after 90 minutes idle anyway, but a running server costs money. Stopping does not delete your work. It is like turning off your computer.
From the JupyterLab tab, choose one of these:

File → Log Out
File → Hub Control Panel → Stop My Server







Tip



Lost the JupyterLab tab? Go to https://workshop.nmfs-openscapes.2i2c.cloud/hub/home.

title: Log in to the JupyterHub
text:
If the server crashes
This can happen when many people use a lot of memory at once. Go to File → Hub Control Panel, click Stop My Server, then Start My Server. You will not lose work, unless you were in the middle of uploading a file.

title: Log in to the JupyterHub
text:
Getting help

Ask in the hackathon channel, or ask a helper in the room.
Problem with this tutorial? Open an issue in ocean-icechunks/2026-ioos-hackathon.

Adapted from NMFS HackDays 2025: Intro to JupyterHubs.

title: Find your way around JupyterLab
text: You need three things in JupyterLab for this hackathon. The terminal is where your coding agent runs. The file browser shows what the agent changed. Notebooks are where you run and check its work.

title: Find your way around JupyterLab
text:
The Launcher
The Launcher opens notebooks, terminals and files. If you do not see it, choose File → New Launcher, or click the blue + at the top left.

title: Find your way around JupyterLab
text:
The terminal
Click Terminal in the Launcher, or choose File → New → Terminal. This is where you will start your agent. You only need a few commands yourself:



Command
What it does




pwd
Shows which folder you are in


ls
Lists the files here (ls -a also shows hidden ones)


cd folder
Moves into a folder


cd ..
Moves up one folder


cd ~
Goes back to your home folder



The agent will run most other commands for you, and it asks before it runs anything risky. New to the shell? Try the Software Carpentry shell lesson.

title: Find your way around JupyterLab
text:
The file browser
The folder icon at the far left opens the file browser. Use it to move between folders, make a new one (the folder icon with a +), and right-click a file to rename or delete it. When an agent writes a file, it shows up here. Open it and read it.

title: Find your way around JupyterLab
text:
Notebooks
Click Python 3 in the Launcher to open a new notebook. A notebook is a list of cells, and each cell is either code or Markdown.

Run a cell: press Shift + Enter.
Run all cells: use the Run menu.
Add a cell: click the + in the notebook toolbar.
Change the cell type: use the drop-down in the toolbar (Code / Markdown).

To open a notebook that someone else wrote, or that the agent wrote, double-click it in the file browser.

title: Find your way around JupyterLab
text:
Installing packages
%pip install package in a notebook cell installs a package for the current session only. It will be gone the next time your server starts. If something should always be there, ask for it to be added to the hub image.
Adapted from NMFS HackDays 2025: Intro to JupyterLab.

title: Git and GitHub, with an agent
text:
Your hackathon work lives in a GitHub repository, so you need a GitHub account. That matters more than usual here: the workshop hub is deleted a week after the hackathon, and GitHub is where your work survives. Git is a lot to learn in one week, and you do not have to: your agent can run the git commands for you. You make the decisions (what to save, when to share it, and whether a change is right), and the agent types the commands.
To do that, the agent needs to reach GitHub as you. You set that up once, with gh auth login.
crumbs: Git and GitHub, with an agent

title: Git and GitHub, with an agent
text:
Why gh auth login?
gh is GitHub’s command-line tool, and it is already installed on the hub. Logging in with it does two things:

git can push and pull over HTTPS without asking you for a password, because gh stores the credential for it.
gh itself can open pull requests, read issues and check on a repository. Agents use it all the time.

Everything the agent does through gh is done in your name, so decide how much it can reach.
crumbs: Git and GitHub, with an agent

title: Git and GitHub, with an agent
text:
Choose how much access

Token for one repository (safer)Full access


The agent can push to your hackathon repository and nothing else.

Go to https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new.
Token name: JupyterHub agent, IOOS hackathon. Expiration: a few days after the hackathon.
Repository access: Only select repositories, then pick your project repository.
Repository permissions: set Contents, Pull requests and Issues to Read and write. Leave the rest at No access.
Click Generate token and copy it. GitHub shows it only once.

Then, in a terminal, run gh auth login and answer:

Where do you use GitHub? GitHub.com
Preferred protocol? HTTPS
Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials? Yes
How would you like to authenticate? Paste an authentication token



The agent can do anything you can on GitHub, in every repository you can reach, including private ones.
In a terminal, run gh auth login and answer:

Where do you use GitHub? GitHub.com
Preferred protocol? HTTPS
Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials? Yes
How would you like to authenticate? Login with a web browser

It prints a one-time code. Open the link, paste the code, and approve.



Check that it worked:
gh auth status
crumbs: Git and GitHub, with an agent

title: Git and GitHub, with an agent
text:
Tell git who you are
Commits need a name and an email. Do this once:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
Use the email on your GitHub account. If you would rather keep it private, use the noreply address shown at https://github.com/settings/emails.
crumbs: Git and GitHub, with an agent

title: Git and GitHub, with an agent
text:
Let the agent do git
Ask for the outcome you want, not the command. For example:







You want to…
Say to the agent




Get a copy of a repository
“Clone github.com/ocean-icechunks/2026-ioos-hackathon into my home folder.”


See what you changed
“What have I changed since the last commit?”


Save your work
“Make a new branch and commit these changes with a clear message.”


Share it
“Push the branch and open a pull request. Explain what changed in the description.”


Catch up with your team
“Pull the latest changes from main and tell me what is new.”


Recover from a mess
“Git says there is a merge conflict. Explain what happened before you fix anything.”



Three habits keep this safe:

Work on a branch, and merge through a pull request. Ask the agent never to push to main.
Read the change before it is committed. Ask “show me the diff” if the agent does not.
Never let credentials into a commit. Keys and tokens belong in environment variables or in a file listed in .gitignore. The ocean-icechunks skill already insists on this.

title: Why virtual Icechunk?
text:
So many NetCDF files

CEFI MOM6 Northeast Pacific hindcast on the PSL THREDDS server: page 1 of 17.
820 files, from one model, one hindcast, one region, and one release.


Ocean model output comes as thousands of NetCDF files, one per variable per year (or per day). Which files do I need? Which variables? A time series means opening hundreds of them.

title: Why virtual Icechunk?
section: Users want a product, not a pile of files
text:
Users want a product, not a pile of files


A cloud-optimized dataset that is linked to the underlying files hides the file structure. The user opens one dataset, with every variable and the full time range, and never sees a file name. We deliver a product.

title: Why virtual Icechunk?
section: Why not just download the files, or use THREDDS?
text:
Why not just download the files, or use THREDDS?


Downloading

Gigabytes to get the one slice you need
Copies on every laptop, all out of date
Hours of scripting before any science

Data servers

Cap large requests (PSL THREDDS: 500 MB each)
Fail under load (“NetCDF: DAP failure”)


Object storage (S3, Google Cloud, Azure)

Serves byte ranges, not whole files
Spreads requests across many machines, so parallel readers do not queue behind each other
In practice, as many connections as you can throw at it



THREDDS has one server, and every request goes through it. Object storage is built to serve huge numbers of concurrent requests for pieces of objects. That is what a cloud-optimized reader needs.

title: Why virtual Icechunk?
text:
From minutes to seconds


Resampling a 2-D CEFI MOM6 NEP variable: THREDDS vs. a virtual store in Earthmover Arraylake. Holmes, ESIP, July 2026.

title: Why virtual Icechunk?
text:
Bering Sea snow crab, 1994–2015
306 TB of HYCOM reanalysis · opens in ~1 s · nothing downloaded






Open in Colab →

Run all cells. The map is the cold pool on the eastern Bering Sea shelf. The time series is the box-mean bottom temperature and the fraction of the box below 2 °C. The metadata comes from Source Cooperative, and every value is read by byte range from HYCOM’s NetCDF files on AWS Open Data.

title: Why virtual Icechunk?
text:
VirtualiZarr: no reprocessing

Keep the data as it is. The NetCDF files stay where the provider put them.
Build a catalog of chunks. For every chunk: which file, at what byte offset, and how long.
Save the catalog as one Zarr dataset. Readers open that, and read the bytes straight from the original files.


If the files are compatible (the same grid, chunking and encoding), there is nothing to rewrite.


This is the big change. We used to have to convert everything to Zarr, which meant a second copy of petabytes. Virtual references point at the originals.

title: Why virtual Icechunk?
section: New tools make this much easier
text:
New tools make this much easier

VirtualiZarr 2: reads NetCDF/HDF5 metadata and builds the chunk catalog
Icechunk 2: stores the catalog, with versions and commits, like git for data
Coding agents + ocean-icechunks-skills: plan, build, check and document a store for you


A year ago this took a specialist days of trial and error. Now the libraries handle the hard parts, and an agent with the skill knows the gotchas.

title: Why virtual Icechunk?
text:
Make your own virtual store

5 NOAA NDVI NetCDF files on AWS
303 MB of data, left in place
54 kB Icechunk store

Open in Colab →

Seven short steps: find the files, tell VirtualiZarr how to reach them, open one, combine five, write and commit, reopen as a reader, plot real data. Measured on 2026-11-13.

title: The basic pipeline
text:
Six steps









Step
What happens




1
Find the files
List the NetCDF files you want in the store


2
Say how to reach them
An object store, a registry and a parser for the file format


3
Open one file virtually
Read its metadata only. The big arrays stay where they are


4
Combine compatible files
Join them along time into one virtual dataset


5
Write and commit
Save the chunk references to an Icechunk repository


6
Reopen and read
Open the store as a reader would, and read real values




This is exactly the NDVI notebook from chapter 1, so anyone who ran it has already done all six steps. The code on the next slides was run end to end on 2026-11-13 (icechunk 2.3.1, virtualizarr 2.8.0).

title: The basic pipeline
text:
1 · Find the files
import s3fs

fs = s3fs.S3FileSystem(anon=True)          # public bucket, no credentials
urls = [f"s3://{p}" for p in sorted(fs.ls("noaa-cdr-ndvi-pds/data/2000"))[:5]]
Five daily files of the NOAA AVHRR NDVI Climate Data Record, January 1–5, 2000.

title: The basic pipeline
text:
2 · Say how to reach them
from obstore.store import from_url
from obspec_utils.registry import ObjectStoreRegistry
from virtualizarr.parsers import HDFParser

bucket = "s3://noaa-cdr-ndvi-pds/"
store = from_url(bucket, region="us-east-1", skip_signature=True)
registry = ObjectStoreRegistry({bucket: store})   # URLs starting with bucket -> this store
parser = HDFParser()                              # NetCDF4 is HDF5 inside

Pick the parser that matches the file format: HDFParser for NetCDF4/HDF5, NetCDF3Parser for classic NetCDF, and others for DMR++, Zarr and FITS. The audit in chapter 4 tells you which one.

title: The basic pipeline
text:
3 · Open one file virtually
from virtualizarr import open_virtual_dataset

coords = ["time", "latitude", "longitude"]
vds = open_virtual_dataset(url=urls[0], parser=parser, registry=registry,
                           loadable_variables=coords)
NDVI   (time, latitude, longitude) int16 52MB ManifestArray<shape=(1, 3600, 7200) ...>

Small coordinates are loaded. Big arrays become ManifestArrays: lists of where each chunk sits (file, byte offset, length). No data is downloaded.

title: The basic pipeline
text:
4 · Combine compatible files
import xarray as xr

vds_list = [
    open_virtual_dataset(url=u, parser=parser, registry=registry, loadable_variables=coords)
    .drop_vars(["nv", "ncrs", "crs"], errors="ignore")
    for u in urls
]
combined = xr.concat(vds_list, dim="time", data_vars="minimal", coords="minimal",
                     compat="override", combine_attrs="override")

“Compatible” means the same dimensions, shape apart from time, chunk grid, dtype and codecs. Files that differ cannot share one virtual array. The keyword arguments stop xarray from trying to compare virtual arrays, which it cannot do. The dropped variables are small CRS and bounds-dimension variables that get in the way of the join.

title: The basic pipeline
text:
5 · Write and commit
import icechunk

config = icechunk.RepositoryConfig.default()
config.set_virtual_chunk_container(icechunk.VirtualChunkContainer(
    url_prefix=bucket, store=icechunk.s3_store(region="us-east-1", anonymous=True)))

storage = icechunk.local_filesystem_storage("ndvi-icechunk")
repo = icechunk.Repository.create(storage, config)
repo.save_config()
combined["time"].encoding["chunks"] = (len(combined.time),)   # one chunk for time
session = repo.writable_session("main")
combined.vz.to_icechunk(session.store)
session.commit("Five days of NDVI CDR, January 2000")

The virtual chunk container tells Icechunk that some chunks live outside the store, under this prefix, and how to reach them. save_config makes that setting part of the store, so readers get it too. Commits work like git: each one is a snapshot you can go back to.

title: The basic pipeline
text:
6 · Reopen and read real data
creds = icechunk.containers_credentials(
    {bucket: icechunk.s3_credentials(anonymous=True)})
reader = icechunk.Repository.open(icechunk.local_filesystem_storage("ndvi-icechunk"),
                                  authorize_virtual_chunk_access=creds)
ds = xr.open_zarr(reader.readonly_session("main").store, consolidated=False, chunks={})

ds["NDVI"].sel(latitude=slice(50, 40), longitude=slice(-126, -114)).isel(time=0).plot()

Always check from a fresh read-only session, and read real values, not just metadata. That is the reader’s path, and it is where problems show up.

title: The basic pipeline
section: From your laptop to the cloud
text:
From your laptop to the cloud
Only step 5’s storage line changes.







Where the store lives
Storage




A local folder
icechunk.local_filesystem_storage("ndvi-icechunk")


Amazon S3
icechunk.s3_storage(bucket="my-bucket", prefix="ndvi-icechunk", region="us-west-2", from_env=True)


Google Cloud Storage
icechunk.gcs_storage(bucket="my-bucket", prefix="ndvi-icechunk", from_env=True)


Published on Source Cooperative
Write with icechunk.s3_storage(...) and your write keys; readers open it with icechunk.http_storage("https://data.source.coop/<account>/<store>")



The NetCDF files never move.

title: Building a virtual Icechunk store
section: Our skill builds up to production
text:
Our skill builds up to production








Step
You get
It must




1 · Plan
plan.md: files, layout, decisions
Be reviewed by you before any code


2 · Smoke test
A notebook that builds a local store from a few files
Reopen it read-only and read real values


3 · Production
A build script: settings at the top, batches, commits, restart
Survive being interrupted; tag the result


4 · Docs
A README, a loading example, the tested environment
Let a stranger open the store with no help



It stops for your review between steps.

title: Building a virtual Icechunk store
section: What the agent needs from you
text:
What the agent needs from you
It cannot guess these. Put them in your first prompt:

Where the files are, and how to get in: a bucket, a THREDDS catalog, an API; public or which credentials
Which files: products, variables, years
Where the store goes: a bucket you can write to. Write credentials go in the environment, never in the chat
Who will read it: Python users, a browser viewer, users outside one cloud region
Built once, or kept up to date as new files arrive

title: Building a virtual Icechunk store
section: What the skill works out from your files
text:
What the skill works out from your files
It will propose these, and ask you to confirm:

One store, or several? The goal is one store with all the variables. Files on different grids or encodings force groups or separate stores
How the files fit together: joined along time, variables in separate files merged
What to load, what to keep virtual: coordinates loaded, science arrays left virtual
Metadata fixes to follow CF conventions


The files usually decide these. You can still ask “why?”, and override.

title: Building a virtual Icechunk store
section: Telling the agent to build it
text:
Telling the agent to build it

“Build a virtual Icechunk store of the NDVI files in s3://noaa-cdr-ndvi-pds/data/ (public, us-east-1) for 2000–2024. Publish it to my Source Cooperative repository my-org/ndvi; my write keys are in environment variables. Python users and a browser viewer will read it. Start with the plan.”

Then, one session per step:

“The plan is approved. Write the smoke-test notebook.” (builds a local test store)
“The smoke test passed. Write the production build script.” (writes to your bucket)
“Write the README and a loading example.”

title: Building a virtual Icechunk store
text:
Authenticating to your bucket
The agent writes to your bucket with your credentials. Tell it where they are:







Destination
Typical credentials




Amazon S3
An AWS profile, or AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in the environment


Google Cloud Storage
A service-account key file, named in GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS


Source Cooperative
Temporary S3 keys from your repository’s View credentials page. They expire



Not sure? Ask it:

“Help me set up write access to my Source Cooperative repository. Do not print my keys, and do not save them in any file in this repository.”


The smoke test always writes to a local store first: the skill never points a test at the real destination. Only the production build writes to the bucket. Keys go in environment variables or a credentials file outside the repository, and never into a notebook, a script or the chat.
